title: National Maritime Union of America v. Commander, Military Sealift Command
lead: Unions challenge contracting out of Navy ship operations, but success on an internal-conflict standing issue does not cure the wage claim’s causal gaps or the other claims’ merits.

actors.name: Three plaintiff unions
actors.role: Representatives of government mariners and Marine Transport employees, but not winning-contractor employees.

actors.name: Military Sealift Command
actors.role: Navy authority awarding the contract and setting appeal and employment-preference rules.

actors.name: Marine Transport Lines
actors.role: Initial tentative winner displaced after solicitation revision.

actors.name: Lavino Shipping
actors.role: Final lowest bidder and awarded contractor.

proceedings: The government rescinded its initial tentative award, revised the solicitation, and awarded Lavino the contract.
The District Court dismissed the unions’ cross-motion action for lack of standing.
The D.C. Circuit rejected automatic disqualification for member conflicts but affirmed judgment for defendants on claim-specific grounds.
limits: The opinion’s associational-standing discussion was not an overall union victory. It did not decide the Service Contract Act zone-of-interests issue or all threshold issues on the other claims, and its regulatory and standing terminology is historical.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: The Navy compares civil-service operation with private bids
sections.cue: How did an absent wage schedule survive a revised solicitation?
paragraphs: The Navy’s Military Sealift Command operated twelve government oceanographic ships with permanent and temporary civil-service mariners. Under procedures implementing Office of Management and Budget Circular A-76, it compared public costs with private bids. The initial solicitation omitted Service Contract Act wages, and Marine Transport Lines received a tentative award. Employee administrative appeals were denied.

The government then concluded the Act applied, rescinded the award, and sought new bids and a revised public estimate. Marine Transport unsuccessfully challenged that step in a separate suit. The revised terms required Labor Department-determined wages and benefits retroactive to award, but the Department lacked timely data, so no actual schedule appeared. Lavino Shipping Company was lowest and won.

The Command denied another appeal because the available issues could have been raised earlier. It limited first-refusal jobs to displaced permanent mariners, protecting career workers from competition by temporary employees in a tight labor market.

sections.title: The unions seek rebidding and alternative employment protections
sections.cue: Why were their members’ interests divided?
paragraphs: Three plaintiff unions, including National Maritime Union of America, represented government mariners and Marine Transport employees, not Lavino workers. They sought injunction, vacatur, and rebidding after a wage determination, or alternatively another appeal and first-refusal rights for temporary mariners. Expanding temporary workers’ preference could reduce permanent workers’ opportunities. Other unions intervened for defendants.

On cross-motions the District Court dismissed for lack of standing. It found plaintiffs outside the wage statute’s zone because they did not represent the successful contractor’s workers and regarded A-76 as internal management without private protected interests. The unions appealed.

sections.title: Bork rejects automatic defeat from internal disagreement
sections.cue: What condition still had to be satisfied?
paragraphs: Judge Bork wrote for a panel also including Judges Starr and D. H. Ginsburg. Applying Hunt, the panel required member standing, germaneness, and no need for individual participation. Employment opportunities were germane. It did not need to classify conflicts as a fourth requirement or part of the participation condition.

UAW v. Brock suggested that conflicts did not automatically bar association suits, although its treatment was not wholly clear. Independently, associations routinely resolve policy disagreements through internal procedures, and members accept collective positions sometimes unfavorable to themselves. Mere dissent did not establish improper representation.

Intervention and organizational-process challenges could protect dissenters; exclusive bargaining power might create fair-representation duties, not implicated here. The court neither declared dissenters individually bound nor relied on a guarantee against later preclusion. The holding remained conditional on individual members possessing standing.

sections.title: The wage claim fails because injury is not tied to the missing schedule
sections.cue: Why could the unions not assert the losing bidder’s rights?
paragraphs: The Act protected contractor employees’ wages, not civil-service wages or losing-bidder opportunities. These unions did not represent holders of the statutory wage right. Their suggested interest in organizing Lavino workers also conflicted with seeking cancellation of Lavino’s contract.

Lost employment was real injury, but the causal and remedial chain from absent schedules was speculative. Lavino already owed eventual prevailing rates retroactively. Nothing showed a schedule would change the winner. Marine Transport was not a party, might not rebid, and had not explained changed cost assumptions; public operating costs did not turn on the Act.

A disappointed bidder could assert its own fair-procurement right, redressed by a lawful new process without guaranteed victory, and clarify willingness and pricing. That right belonged to Marine Transport, not the unions. The opinion noted limits for bidders outside active consideration and distinguished requests for rebidding from requests for a direct award. The panel rejected this claim for Article III traceability and redressability, expressly leaving the statutory zone issue undecided.

sources.pinpoint: Service Contract Act claim; 824 F.2d at 1234–1238 & nn.10–14

sections.title: The directly denied appeal and preference claims fail substantively
sections.cue: What judgment does the court affirm?
paragraphs: Denial of an appeal or first-refusal right directly injured members and could be redressed, satisfying Article III for those claims. The court assumed remaining zone, cause-of-action, and justiciability issues because the claims failed even under the less demanding proposed review standard on undisputed facts.

Regulations required an appeal opportunity, not a futile second one. Appealable matters involved contracting out, not competing bidders or management choices; the public estimate and public-private gap had not materially changed, and unions already had reason and opportunity to object.

Temporary workers’ handbook eligibility did not establish unconditional preference. The court deferred to the Command’s reading and found protecting permanent careers from added competition reasonable. It ordered no equal preference rights.

On July 31, 1987, Bork, Starr, and D. H. Ginsburg unanimously affirmed judgment for defendants with no separate opinions. Internal conflicts alone did not bar association, but missing individual standing and unsuccessful merits still defeated the suit.

sources.pinpoint: Administrative appeal; First refusal; Judgment; 824 F.2d at 1238–1240
